candidates.attacker_control: Attack vector 1 (write): authenticated admin (admin_token header/query, or a valid one-shot `temp_token` such as the one embedded in backup download links, since AbstractAuthenticationFilter.checkForTempToken bypasses doAuthenticate for any admin URL) uploads a crafted ZIP with entry names like `x/../../../../<abs target>` to POST /api/admin/themes/upload; the ZIP file name only needs to end in `.zip`. Attack vector 2 (read/write): the admin passes `path=<theme-absolute-path>/../../../<file>` to GET/PUT /api/admin/themes/files/content (`@RequestParam path` / ThemeContentParam.path, no validation); the theme's absolute path is disclosed by GET /api/admin/themes/{id} (ThemeProperty.themePath) and the file tree API.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: AdminAuthenticationFilter covers /api/admin/* with no theme exclusions (HaloConfiguration.java:155-171), so by default these endpoints are not anonymous; auth-enabled defaults to true (HaloProperties.java:37). The unzip routine creates a fresh empty temp dir (mustBeEmpty) and only deletes tempPath afterwards, so nothing rolls back escaped writes. Absolute ZIP entry names are correctly rejected (resolve returns the absolute name, which fails startsWith), so the bypass requires relative names — which is sufficient. tryToSkipZipParentFolder/copyFolder are not needed for the write step. ThemeContentParam has no bean validation, so `path` reaches the service unchanged. No runtime execution was performed; Path.startsWith semantics (prefix comparison of name elements; `..` treated as an ordinary element) and OS-side `..` resolution were verified against source/JDK contract only.
candidates.impact: Bypass of the intended 'stay inside the theme/temp directory' boundary, giving the service account arbitrary filesystem read and write: read secrets (e.g. ~/.halo/application.yaml with datasource credentials, other users' files the process can read), overwrite application config/templates/static assets served by the app (persistent XSS or token theft from the admin UI), or plant files consumed by other processes. Under the default Docker deployment (root, no USER) a write primitive is a strong path to full host/container compromise (e.g. overwriting config or startup/cron-consumed files), i.e. theme-management rights escalate to RCE-level impact.
candidates.prerequisites: Halo authentication enabled (default `halo.auth.enabled=true`) and the attacker holds a valid admin (or one-shot temp) token, i.e. an authenticated admin or a leaked token. For vector 1, the ZIP entry's parent directory must exist or the archive must first include a directory entry for it; the process account must be able to write the target. For vector 2, a theme must exist/be activated so its absolute path can be obtained. Impact scales with the service account: the shipped Dockerfile has no USER directive (runs as root) and mounts the work directory.
candidates.root_cause: FileUtils.checkDirectoryTraversal(parentPath, pathToCheck) does not normalize pathToCheck before the containment test: `if (pathToCheck.startsWith(parentPath.normalize())) return;` (FileUtils.java:299). Path.startsWith compares leading name elements only, and `..` is an ordinary name element, so a path such as <parent>/x/../../../../target equals the parent as a prefix and passes the check even though the OS-resolved target is outside the parent. Because in unzip() the checked path is built as targetPath.resolve(zipEntry.getName()) (FileUtils.java:101) and any relative entry name is appended after the target path's own elements, *every* relative ZIP entry name passes, including names containing `..`; absolute entry names are the only ones rejected. The same helper backs ThemeServiceImpl.checkDirectory(String/themeId, absoluteName) (ThemeServiceImpl.java:729-743), invoked by getTemplateContent/saveTemplateContent with client-supplied absolute paths.
candidates.title: Directory-traversal check bypass in FileUtils.checkDirectoryTraversal enables Zip Slip arbitrary file write and theme-editor arbitrary file read/write
candidates.trace: 1) POST /api/admin/themes/upload -> ThemeServiceImpl.upload (ThemeServiceImpl.java:394) validates only the `.zip` suffix, creates tempPath and target themeTempPath, then calls FileUtils.unzip(zis, themeTempPath) (line 417). 2) FileUtils.unzip iterates entries: entryPath = targetPath.resolve(zipEntry.getName()) (FileUtils.java:101); FileUtils.checkDirectoryTraversal(targetPath, entryPath) (line 104). 3) In checkDirectoryTraversal, entryPath.startsWith(targetPath.normalize()) (line 299) is true whenever the entry name is relative — its leading elements are exactly targetPath's elements — so `..` segments later in the name are never evaluated; no ForbiddenException is thrown. 4) Files.createDirectories(entryPath) / Files.copy(zis, entryPath) (lines 106-111) then create/write the OS-resolved path outside the temp folder (e.g. `x/../../../../home/halo/.halo/application.yaml`). Later steps (tryToSkipZipParentFolder/add/getProperty) may fail for a non-theme archive, but the writes already happened and only tempPath is cleaned up in the finally block (lines 423-428). 5) The analogous content API: ThemeController.getContentBy/updateContentBy (ThemeController.java:61-81) -> ThemeServiceImpl.getTemplateContent/saveTemplateContent -> checkDirectory(absoluteName) -> the same flawed comparison (lines 219/246/731), then Files.readAllBytes/Files.write on the client-provided path.
candidates.unverified: No runtime test, exploit payload, or scanner was run; I could not execute the app or a JDK path experiment. Actual writable targets and impact depend on deployment (Docker image runs as root, but bare-metal/systemd deployments may use a non-root account). Whether earlier upstream versions normalized the child path (i.e. whether this is a regression or long-standing bug) could not be checked without external sources.

coverage_summary: Source scope: 494 model-visible files (407 Java) under src/main; binary-like files are skipped/refused (none encountered as relevant). P1 relation scope: 493 files indexed, 407 parsed Java files, 1 omitted file, 3,042 symbols, 4,871 edges, 5,813 unresolved calls; control-flow, data-flow and semantic resolution are not implemented, and the index is explicitly partial, so all call/containment edges were treated as navigational hints and re-verified in source text. In-depth review covered: security filters and context (Abstract/Admin/Api/Content filters, SecurityUtils, AuthenticationArgumentResolver), HaloConfiguration/WebMvcAutoConfiguration/CorsFilter, theme service and controller, FileUtils/all utils (FilenameUtils, MarkdownUtils, HttpClientUtils, WordPressMigrateUtils), backup service/controller, admin service/controller, attachment/file handlers (LocalFileHandler, AttachmentServiceImpl), migrate handlers (Old/WordPress/CnBlogs) and MigrateController/RecoveryController, comment services/listeners, OptionService, install controller, and representative content/admin controllers. Not exhaustively reviewed: most entity/DTO/repository classes, minified admin JS/CSS and bundled theme assets (only text-searched), FreeMarker templates/themes, and the remaining content HTML controllers such as ContentArchiveController/ContentFeedController beyond spot checks. No tests exist in the snapshot to corroborate runtime behavior.
limitations: No code was executed; no tests, scanners, or payloads were run, so all findings are source-level leads, not runtime-confirmed vulnerabilities.

P1 index is partial and syntactic (no CFG/DFG/semantic resolution, 5,813 unresolved calls); reachability and data flow were established by reading source, but end-to-end exploitability was not proven.
Attacker prerequisite for the candidate is an authenticated admin (or a leaked one-shot temp token); anonymous exploitation of the traversal flaw was not found.
Impact assessment depends on the deployment account and writable paths (default Dockerfile runs as root; other deployments may not).
Behavior of Path.startsWith with `..` elements and OS resolution of `..` during file writes is reasoned from the Java contract, not observed.

Repository/upstream history could not be consulted (no sibling versions, patches, or external sources allowed), so it was not possible to confirm whether this is a regression or a long-standing unfixed bug.

rejected_leads.lead: No authentication on /api/admin/migrations/* (HaloConfiguration excludes it; MigrateController has no installed-state check) → anonymous WordPress/old-version import can create published posts/sheets/comments/menus with attacker-controlled content (stored-XSS/defacement potential).
rejected_leads.reason: The exclusion patterns look deliberately designed for pre-install migration (RecoveryController even checks isInstalled), so intent is ambiguous and impact is data injection, not direct file-system compromise; strong but less clear-cut than the traversal bypass. Kept as an unconfirmed lead, not a second candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: IDOR on GET /api/content/journals/{journalId}: JournalServiceImpl/Content JournalController returns journals without filtering JournalType.PUBLIC, so private journals can be read anonymously by ID.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible access-control gap, but default journal types/visibility semantics were not fully verified across the HTML controller and repository, and impact is limited to journal content confidentiality.

rejected_leads.lead: BackupServiceImpl.loadFileAsResource normalizes but does not verify containment (and deleteHaloBackup does not normalize), enabling arbitrary file read/delete via /api/admin/backups/halo/{fileName}.
rejected_leads.reason: Admin-authenticated only; same trust level as the primary candidate but lower technical specificity and no separate root cause beyond path containment.

rejected_leads.lead: HttpClientUtils.createHttpsClient uses a trust-all TrustStrategy plus NoopHostnameVerifier for the shared RestTemplate (theme download, admin assets, password-reset mail path).
rejected_leads.reason: TLS-verification weakness enabling MITM in some flows; requires network-position attacker and no direct server-side secret exposure was traced in source.

rejected_leads.lead: CorsFilter reflects the request Origin and always sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true for /api/*.
rejected_leads.reason: Dangerous pattern, but authentication here is token-in-header/query (no cookie session), so a concrete cross-origin credential-carrying attack was not established from source.

rejected_leads.lead: Password reset flow (AdminServiceImpl.sendResetPasswordCode/resetPasswordByCode): 6-digit code under a single global cache key, 5-minute TTL, unlimited attempts, no rate-limit/lockout on /api/admin/password/code or /password/reset.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires SMTP enabled and knowledge of the admin username+email; brute force of 6 digits is noisy and no source-level proof of reachable account takeover was demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: WordPressMigrateHandler uses new FileInputStream(migrationContent) where migrationContent is the uploaded file's body, treating content as a local path (potential local-file XML read / XXE surface via dom4j SAXReader).
rejected_leads.reason: Reachable unauthenticated through the migration endpoint, but exploitation needs an attacker-known local file that is valid XML with the expected structure; no content-disclosure path to the attacker could be confirmed statically.

summary: Reviewed Halo 1.1.3-beta.3 (Spring Boot CMS, 407 Java files). The strongest source-backed issue is a broken directory-traversal check in FileUtils.checkDirectoryTraversal: it compares the *un-normalized* child path via Path.startsWith, so any relative path containing ".." is accepted. This makes the check a no-op for ZIP entry names (Zip Slip in FileUtils.unzip, reachable from theme ZIP upload/update) and bypassable for the theme template-content API (arbitrary file read/write). One candidate is submitted; all reachable entry points require an admin token (or a valid one-shot temp token), so this is privilege escalation from theme management to filesystem access of the service account (root in the default Docker image), not an anonymous issue.
